Charging Your Electric Motorcycle Across the UK

Understanding the UK's charging network is essential for electric motorcycle touring. While the network is expanding rapidly, it is not yet as ubiquitous or reliable as petrol stations. Knowing which networks to use, which apps to download, and how to plan your charging stops transforms electric touring from stressful to enjoyable.

UK Charging Networks

  • Tesla Supercharger — Now open to non-Tesla vehicles including motorcycles with CCS connectors. Fast and reliable but check the app for motorcycle accessibility as some locations have awkward cable lengths.
  • Gridserve Electric Highway — Found at motorway service stations across the UK. Reliable DC fast charging with contactless payment. Generally motorcycle-accessible.
  • BP Pulse — Widespread network with chargers at many BP forecourts and car parks. Mixed reliability but improving. The app is essential for locating available chargers.
  • Pod Point — Common at supermarkets and retail parks. Mostly AC charging (slower) but useful for topping up while shopping or eating.
  • Osprey Charging — Growing network of fast chargers at convenient locations. Generally well-maintained with contactless payment.

Essential Apps

Zap-Map — The definitive UK charging map showing all networks, charger types, real-time availability, and user reviews. Essential for planning routes and finding chargers. The community updates identify broken chargers quickly.

A Better Route Planner (ABRP) — Route planning app that calculates charging stops based on your bike's range, speed, and battery capacity. It accounts for elevation, weather, and driving style to give realistic range estimates.

Practical Charging Tips

Plan your stops: Unlike petrol touring where you refuel when the tank gets low, electric touring requires planning charging stops in advance. Map your route around charger locations and always have a backup charger identified in case your primary choice is occupied or broken.

Charge to 80 percent: Charging from 80 to 100 percent takes almost as long as charging from 10 to 80 percent. For touring efficiency, charge to 80 and move on rather than waiting for a full battery.

Carry adapters: A Type 2 to three-pin adapter lets you charge from a standard domestic socket in an emergency. It is painfully slow but could save you from being stranded at a remote B&B with no public charger nearby.

Always arrive at a charger with at least 15-20 percent battery remaining. Charger reliability is not guaranteed, and arriving with a dead battery at a broken charger is a deeply stressful situation.

Charging Etiquette

Do not hog chargers once your bike is charged. Move it promptly so the next user can plug in. If a charger has a queue, be patient and courteous. The electric vehicle community is generally friendly and helpful — many car drivers are curious about electric motorcycles and happy to share charger knowledge.
keyTakeaways: Zap-Map is the essential app for finding chargers, checking live availability and spotting broken units.
Charge to 80 percent and move on, as the final 20 percent takes almost as long as the first 70.
Always arrive at a charger with 15-20 percent in reserve in case it is broken or occupied.
Gridserve and Tesla Superchargers are among the most reliable and motorcycle-accessible networks.
Carry a Type 2 to three-pin adapter for slow emergency charging at accommodation.

pros: Motorway rapid-charging coverage is now reasonably comprehensive.
Apps like Zap-Map and ABRP make planning and routing straightforward.

cons: Charger reliability is not guaranteed, so backups must be planned.
Some car-oriented chargers have awkward cable reach or parking for bikes.

faq.q: Which app should I use to find chargers?
faq.a: Zap-Map is the definitive UK charging map, showing every network, charger type, live availability and user reviews that flag broken units quickly. Pair it with A Better Route Planner, which calculates charging stops based on your bike's range, speed and battery capacity while accounting for elevation and weather. Between them you can plan reliable charging stops anywhere in the country.

faq.q: Why should I only charge to 80 percent?
faq.a: Charging from 80 to 100 percent takes almost as long as going from 10 to 80 percent because the charge rate tapers sharply as the battery fills. For touring efficiency it is faster overall to stop at 80 percent and cover more ground between charges. Save the full charge for overnight, when a slower top-up costs you no riding time.

faq.q: What if the charger is broken or occupied?
faq.a: Always arrive with at least 15 to 20 percent battery in reserve and identify a backup charger before you set off, because charger reliability is not guaranteed. Zap-Map's live status and community reports help you spot problems in advance. Arriving with a nearly flat battery at a broken charger is one of the most stressful situations in electric touring.

faq.q: Can I charge from a normal socket?
faq.a: Yes, with a Type 2 to three-pin adapter you can charge from a standard domestic socket, which is useful in an emergency or overnight at a B&B with no public charger. It is painfully slow, adding only a few miles per hour, so treat it as a backup rather than a touring solution. It can still save you from being stranded in a remote area.
